title: Iterators and the Iteration Protocol
description: Master iterables, iterators, iter() and next(), StopIteration signaling, custom iterator classes, and lazy traversal.
learning_objectives: Distinguish between iterables (containers) and iterators (stateful streams)
Drive traversal programmatically using iter(), next(), and default fallbacks
Implement custom iterator classes adhering strictly to the iterator protocol
Execute lazy traversal to stream unbounded datasets in constant O(1) space

sections.title: Iterable vs iterator: Containers and stateful streams
sections.learning_objective: Differentiate between objects that can be iterated and active stream cursors.
sections.markdown: An `iterable` is any object capable of returning its members one at a time. Examples include lists, tuples, dictionaries, and strings. An iterable implements `__iter__()` which returns an iterator. An `iterator` is the stateful stream object itself. It represents a stream of data and implements both `__next__()` and `__iter__()` (which returns `self`). While an iterable like a list can be looped over multiple times, an iterator is exhausted after a single pass.

examples.code:
numbers = [10, 20, 30]
it = iter(numbers)
print('Is list an iterator?', hasattr(numbers, '__next__'))
print('Is it an iterator?', hasattr(it, '__next__'))
print(next(it), next(it))
examples.explanation: Lists have __iter__ but not __next__; calling iter(numbers) produces an iterator with __next__.
examples.expected_output:
Is list an iterator? False
Is it an iterator? True
10 20

key_points: An iterable produces an iterator via __iter__(); it can be iterated multiple times.
An iterator produces values one at a time via __next__() and is consumed once.
sections.checkpoint: What happens when you pass an already exhausted iterator into a for loop?

sections.title: The iter() and next() functions and StopIteration
sections.learning_objective: Drive iteration manually and handle exhaustion safely.
sections.markdown: Python's `for` loop is syntactic sugar over `iter()` and `next()`. The `next(iterator, default)` function requests the next item. When no items remain, `next()` raises a `StopIteration` exception. If a second `default` argument is supplied (e.g. `next(it, None)`), Python returns the default instead of raising `StopIteration`. This provides an elegant way to inspect the first matching element of a stream without raising exceptions.

examples.code:
tokens = iter(['alpha', 'beta'])
print(next(tokens))
print(next(tokens))
# Third call with default avoids exception
print(next(tokens, 'END'))
examples.explanation: Consumes all tokens; passing 'END' as default returns the sentinel without raising StopIteration.

key_points: for loops repeatedly call next() and automatically catch StopIteration.
next(it, default) returns a fallback value when exhausted.
sections.checkpoint: Write a while loop that manually replicates the exact mechanics of a for loop using iter() and next().

sections.title: Implementing custom iterator classes
sections.learning_objective: Build classes adhering to the Python iterator protocol.
sections.markdown:
To build a custom iterator, implement the iterator protocol:
1. `__iter__(self)`: returns `self`.
2. `__next__(self)`: returns the next value, or raises `StopIteration` when the sequence is exhausted.

Maintaining the cursor state inside the instance allows traversing complex data structures (trees, ring buffers, database cursors) with standard Python loops.

examples.explanation: Countdown manages its own decrementing counter, raising StopIteration when reaching zero.

key_points: Custom iterators implement __iter__() returning self and __next__() producing items.
Raising StopIteration signals the end of the sequence.
sections.checkpoint: Why must an iterator's __iter__() method return self?

sections.title: Lazy traversal and memory efficiency
sections.learning_objective: Stream massive datasets without out-of-memory crashes.
sections.markdown: The defining advantage of iterators is lazy evaluation: values are computed or retrieved only when requested. A list of 100 million integers consumes gigabytes of memory. An iterator representing the same sequence generates items on demand, maintaining O(1) auxiliary space regardless of sequence size. Standard library modules like `itertools` provide building blocks (`islice`, `chain`, `cycle`) for building memory-efficient data pipelines.

examples.code:
import itertools

# Infinite counter takes O(1) memory
counter = itertools.count(start=100, step=10)
first_three = list(itertools.islice(counter, 3))
print(first_three)
examples.explanation: itertools.count is an unbounded iterator; islice extracts 3 elements without materializing infinity.

key_points: Iterators compute values lazily, requiring O(1) constant memory.
Itertools provides composable stream combinators like islice and chain.
sections.checkpoint: Contrast loading 10GB of CSV rows into a list vs iterating with an iterator.

sections.title: The two-argument iter() sentinel pattern
sections.learning_objective: Read blocks and streams using sentinel iteration.
sections.markdown: Python's `iter()` function supports a powerful two-argument signature: `iter(callable, sentinel)`. It creates an iterator that repeatedly calls `callable()` with zero arguments on each step until the returned value equals `sentinel`, at which point it terminates. This pattern cleanly solves the traditional "read until EOF or empty block" problem without awkward `while True:` break loops.

examples.code:
import io

stream = io.StringIO('chunk1\nchunk2\n\nchunk3')
# Read lines until empty line sentinel is reached
reader = iter(stream.readline, '\n')
lines = [line.strip() for line in reader]
print('Read before sentinel:', lines)
examples.explanation: iter(stream.readline, '\n') calls readline until an empty newline is encountered.

key_points: iter(callable, sentinel) repeatedly invokes the callable until it produces the sentinel value.
Eliminates boilerplate while True loops for stream reading.
sections.checkpoint: How does iter(file.readline, '') read an entire file until end-of-file?

sections.title: Interview check and practice
sections.learning_objective: Review iterator interview questions and practice streaming in Coding Arena.
sections.markdown:
Iterator mechanics are essential for designing scalable systems and backend streaming pipelines.

### Oral Interview Questions
1. *Can an iterator be reset back to the beginning?*
   *(No. An iterator is a forward-only stream. Once exhausted, it cannot be reset. To re-iterate, you must obtain a new iterator from the underlying iterable).*
2. *What is the relationship between iterators and generators in Python?*
   *(All generators are iterators, but not all iterators are generator functions. Generators are an ergonomic syntax for creating iterators using yield).* 
3. *How does Python handle memory when passing an iterator to sum()?*

### Code Trace Challenge
Trace this snippet:
```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
it = iter(nums)
print(list(it))
print(list(it))
```
The first `list(it)` exhausts the iterator and prints `[1, 2, 3]`. The second `list(it)` receives an empty exhausted stream, printing `[]`!

### Common Interview Trap
Assuming an iterator can be reused. Passing an iterator to two sequential loops means the second loop never runs because the iterator was already exhausted by the first.

### Arena Practice Problems
Practice iterator traversal in Coding Arena:
- `python-flatten-list`: Iterating through nested sequences
- `python-largest-product`: Sliding traversal over sequential elements
- `python-matrix-spiral`: State-based coordinates traversal

examples.code:
data = iter([1, 2, 3])
first = list(data)
second = list(data)
print(f'First: {first}, Second: {second}')
examples.explanation: Demonstrates that exhausted iterators yield no more items on subsequent iterations.

key_points: Iterators are stateful, forward-only, and single-use.
Convert an iterator to a list if you need to access elements repeatedly.
sections.checkpoint: Explain how itertools.tee(it, 2) creates two independent iterators from a single stream.

summary: Iterables implement __iter__() returning an iterator; iterators implement __next__() producing items.
The iteration protocol terminates by raising StopIteration.
next(it, default) cleanly consumes stream elements with a fallback value.
Custom iterators maintain state internally across __next__() invocations.
Lazy traversal streams unbounded or massive datasets in constant O(1) memory.
interview_takeaways: Iterators cannot be rewound or re-read; they are single-pass streams.
Use iter(callable, sentinel) to cleanly read data streams until a terminator.
Choose iterators over lists when memory efficiency dominates speed requirements.
common_mistakes: Attempting to reuse an exhausted iterator in a second loop
Confusing an iterable container (list) with an iterator cursor
Forgetting to implement __iter__ on a custom iterator class
Calling next() without catching StopIteration or providing a default value
